meaning: can do / is able to do

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The potential form expresses ability or possibility — 'can do X'. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding られる (食べる → 食べられる). Godan verbs change the final u-row kana to the corresponding e-row kana and add る (行く → 行ける, 話す → 話せる). In modern colloquial Japanese, ら is often dropped from ichidan potential forms (食べれる instead of 食べられる) — this is called ら抜き言葉 and is widely used but grammatically nonstandard. The irregular する becomes できる, and くる becomes こられる.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add られる. Godan: u-row → e-row + る. Irregular: する → できる, くる → こられる.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
ら-less forms (食べれる, 見れる) are colloquial and widely used but grammatically nonstandard.
The object of a potential verb takes が (or sometimes を): 日本語が話せる ('can speak Japanese').
できる is a standalone word meaning 'can do'; it is the potential form of する and also used for general ability.

examples.jp: 日本語が話せます。
examples.en: I can speak Japanese.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語が<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>せます。

examples.jp: この魚は食べられますか。
examples.en: Can you eat this fish? / Is this fish edible?
examples.furi: この<ruby>魚<rt>うお</rt></ruby>は<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べられますか。

examples.jp: 早く起きられない。
examples.en: I can't get up early. (plain)
examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きられない。

meaning: is done (passive); also expresses adversity / indirect affect

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The passive form expresses that the subject receives an action. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding られる. Godan verbs change the u-row kana to the a-row and add れる. Note that ichidan passive and potential forms are homophones (食べられる can mean 'can eat' or 'is eaten'). Japanese also has a distinctive use of passive to express that something bad or unwanted happened to the speaker — the 'suffering passive' (私は雨に降られた — 'I got rained on').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add られる. Godan: u-row → a-row + れる. Irregular: する → される, くる → こられる.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The passive agent (the one who did the action) takes に: 先生に叱られた ('I was scolded by the teacher').
Suffering passive: even intransitive verbs can be used passively to express adversity (雨に降られる, 友達に来られる).

examples.jp: 先生に褒められました。
examples.en: I was praised by the teacher.
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>褒<rt>ほ</rt></ruby>められました。

examples.jp: 友達に手紙を読まれました。
examples.en: My letter was read by my friend. (often with a suffering nuance)
examples.furi: <ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>まれました。

examples.jp: ドアが開けられた。
examples.en: The door was opened. (plain)
examples.furi: ドアが<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けられた。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The causative form expresses that the subject makes or lets someone else do an action. Ichidan verbs form it by dropping る and adding させる. Godan verbs change the u-row kana to the a-row and add せる. The distinction between 'make' (forced) and 'let' (permitted) depends on context and the particle marking the causee: を often implies force, に often implies permission.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add させる. Godan: u-row → a-row + せる. Irregular: する → させる, くる → こさせる.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The causee is marked with に (permission) or を (force/coercion), though the distinction is not always strict.
The combined causative-passive (食べさせられる — 'be made to eat') is N3.

examples.jp: 先生は学生に本を読ませました。
examples.en: The teacher made/had the students read the book.
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>ませました。

examples.jp: 子供を遊ばせました。
examples.en: I let the children play.
examples.furi: <ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>を<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>ばせました。

examples.jp: 母は弟に野菜を食べさせました。
examples.en: My mother made my little brother eat vegetables.
examples.furi: <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>は<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べさせました。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: Vた + ことがある expresses past experience — 'have (ever) done X'. It refers to whether the speaker has done something at any point in the past, not a specific event. The negative is ことがない ('have never done'). Combined with a question, it asks whether the listener has done something.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-た form + ことがある (polite: ことがあります)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
ことがない = 'have never done'.
Used for life experiences, not recent specific events. For recent past, just use the plain past form.
Time markers like 子供の時 ('when I was a child') or 一度も ('not even once') are common with this construction.

examples.jp: 日本に行ったことがあります。
examples.en: I have been to Japan.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>ぎょう</rt></ruby>ったことがあります。

examples.jp: 寿司を食べたことがありますか。
examples.en: Have you ever eaten sushi?
examples.furi: 寿司を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べたことがありますか。

examples.jp: 一度も会ったことがない。
examples.en: I have never met (them) even once.
examples.furi: <ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>も<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>ったことがない。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: つもり attached after a dictionary-form verb expresses the speaker's intention or plan to do something. It is stronger than a vague thought — it implies the speaker has already decided. The negative can be either ないつもり ('intend not to') or つもりはない ('don't have any intention'). It is used primarily for first-person intention; for third-person, other constructions (と言っている) are preferred.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb (dictionary form) + つもり(です)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Negative 1: Vない + つもり — 'intend not to X' (I have decided not to)
Negative 2: Vる + つもりはない — 'don't have any intention of X' (stronger denial).
For something already done, use Vた + つもり ('I thought I did X' — implying mistaken belief).

examples.jp: 来年、日本に行くつもりです。
examples.en: I'm planning to go to Japan next year.
examples.furi: <ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりです。

examples.jp: お酒を飲まないつもりです。
examples.en: I intend not to drink alcohol.
examples.furi: お<ruby>酒<rt>さけ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>まないつもりです。

examples.jp: 大学を卒業したら、留学するつもりです。
examples.en: I plan to study abroad after I graduate from university.
examples.furi: <ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>したら、<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>するつもりです。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: と思う attached after a plain-form clause expresses the speaker's opinion or belief — 'I think that…'. The clause before と must be in plain form, not polite (食べると思う, not 食べますと思う). It is the basic way to express opinions in Japanese and is extremely common. For past belief, use と思った.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form clause + と + 思う (polite: 思います)

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The embedded clause must be in plain form: 高いと思います, not 高いですと思います.
と思っている (resultant state) is used for holding an opinion over time, especially for third-person opinions: 彼はそう思っている ('he thinks so').
For intention, Vよう + と思う ('I'm thinking of doing X') combines with the volitional form.

examples.jp: 明日は雨が降ると思います。
examples.en: I think it will rain tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

examples.jp: 彼はいい人だと思う。
examples.en: I think he's a good person. (plain)
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はいい<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う。

examples.jp: このレストランは高いと思います。
examples.en: I think this restaurant is expensive.
examples.furi: このレストランは<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

related: Plain form + だろう / でしょう

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: と言う has two related uses: (1) quotation — 'someone says/said that ___' — attached after a plain-form clause, and (2) naming — 'is called ___' — used to give the name of something. In the quotation use, the cited content is in plain form. The past form と言った means 'said that'. と言います is the polite form.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form clause + と + 言う. For naming: 'Xという + noun' (e.g., 田中という人 — 'a person called Tanaka').

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Use plain form in the embedded clause.
The naming pattern X という Y is very productive: 'anime' in Japanese is アニメ and you might say アニメというもの ('the thing called anime').

examples.jp: 彼は明日来ると言いました。
examples.en: He said he would come tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いました。

examples.jp: 田中という人を知っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know a person called Tanaka?
examples.furi: 田中という<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っていますか。

examples.jp: 先生は「静かにしなさい」と言いました。
examples.en: The teacher said, 'Be quiet.'
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は「<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かにしなさい」と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>いました。

point: Plain form + だろう / でしょう
meaning: probably / I guess / it will probably be

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: だろう (plain) and でしょう (polite) express the speaker's conjecture or guess about something — 'probably', 'I think', 'I guess'. They attach to the plain form of verbs, い-adjectives, and nouns/na-adjectives. でしょう is also used with rising intonation to seek the listener's agreement or confirmation ('right?').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form verb/い-adj/noun + だろう (plain) or でしょう (polite). For nouns and な-adjectives, attach directly without だ: 学生でしょう, not 学生だでしょう.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Do not include だ before でしょう for noun/na-adjective predicates: 学生でしょう, 静かでしょう.
With rising intonation, でしょう seeks confirmation: いいでしょう？('that's good, right?').
The past form だったろう / だったでしょう means 'would have been / must have been'.

examples.jp: 明日は晴れるでしょう。
examples.en: It will probably be sunny tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れるでしょう。

examples.jp: 彼はもう帰ったでしょう。
examples.en: He's probably already gone home.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったでしょう。

examples.jp: この仕事は大変だろう。
examples.en: This job is probably tough. (plain)
examples.furi: この<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>だろう。

related: Plain form + かもしれない

point: Plain form + かもしれない

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: かもしれない (polite かもしれません) expresses possibility — 'might', 'may', 'perhaps'. It is weaker than だろう/でしょう, indicating less certainty. It attaches to the plain form of verbs, い-adjectives, and noun/na-adjective predicates (without だ).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form verb/adjective/noun + かもしれない (drop だ for nouns and na-adjectives).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
No だ before かもしれない for nouns: 学生かもしれません, not 学生だかもしれません.
Casual contraction: かも (especially at the end: 行くかも — 'might go').

examples.jp: 明日は雨が降るかもしれません。
examples.en: It might rain tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るかもしれません。

examples.jp: 彼は来ないかもしれない。
examples.en: He might not come. (plain)
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ないかもしれない。

examples.jp: あの店はもう閉まっているかもしれません。
examples.en: That shop might already be closed.
examples.furi: あの<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>まっているかもしれません。

related: Plain form + だろう / でしょう

meaning: should be / ought to be / is expected to

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: はず expresses the speaker's expectation based on reasoning or evidence — 'it should be' or 'it ought to be'. Unlike かもしれない (possibility), はず implies stronger certainty; unlike べき (obligation), はず is about expectation rather than what someone should do morally. The negative はずがない means 'there's no way that' — a strong denial.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form verb/adjective/noun + はず(です). For nouns and na-adjectives, use の before はず: 学生のはず, 静かなはず.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Noun + の + はず; な-adjective + な + はず.
はずがない = 'no way that' (strong denial of possibility).
はずだった = 'was supposed to' (but something went wrong).

examples.jp: 彼は今日来るはずです。
examples.en: He should come today.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るはずです。

examples.jp: そんなはずはない。
examples.en: There's no way that can be true. (plain)
examples.furi: そんなはずはない。

examples.jp: 荷物は明日届くはずです。
examples.en: The package should arrive tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>くはずです。

related: Plain form + かもしれない

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: たら is the most versatile Japanese conditional. It attaches to the た-form of a verb (or the かった form of an い-adjective, だった of a noun/na-adjective) and expresses 'if/when X happens'. It can refer to either a single future event ('if X happens' / 'when X happens') or a past event where the speaker discovered something ('when I did X, Y happened'). It's generally the safest conditional to use when learners aren't sure which of たら/ば/と/なら to pick.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-た + ら (食べた → 食べたら). い-adj: かった + ら (高かったら). Noun/な-adj: だった + ら (学生だったら).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Often used for past-tense 'when I did X, I discovered/found Y': 家に帰ったら、誰もいなかった ('when I got home, no one was there').
Can express future 'when/after': 東京に着いたら電話します ('I'll call when I arrive in Tokyo').
For definite future, the main clause can express will/intention/command/request. For past discovery, the main clause is a past event.

examples.jp: 時間があったら、映画を見ます。
examples.en: If I have time, I'll watch a movie.
examples.furi: <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>があったら、<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ます。

examples.jp: 家に帰ったら、手紙が来ていた。
examples.en: When I got home, a letter had come.
examples.furi: <ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったら、<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>らい</rt></ruby>ていた。

examples.jp: お金があったら、新しいパソコンを買いたいです。
examples.en: If I had money, I'd want to buy a new computer.
examples.furi: お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>があったら、<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいパソコンを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いたいです。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The ば-conditional expresses a hypothetical 'if' — typically generic conditions or natural laws. It tends to emphasize the condition itself and is common in proverbs, mathematical statements, and generic claims. For specific contingent plans, たら is more common.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add れば (食べる → 食べれば). Godan: u-row → e-row + ば (行く → 行けば, 飲む → 飲めば). い-adj: drop い, add ければ (高い → 高ければ). Negative: ～なければ. Irregular: する → すれば, くる → くれば.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
ば is preferred for natural or generic conditions ('if you study, you'll understand' — 勉強すればわかる).
The main clause of a ば-sentence usually does not express commands, requests, or invitations. Use たら for those.
The exception is when the subjects differ or the condition is stative.

examples.jp: 毎日勉強すれば、上手になります。
examples.en: If you study every day, you'll become skilled.
examples.furi: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>すれば、<ruby>上手<rt>じょうず</rt></ruby>になります。

examples.jp: 安ければ買います。
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.furi: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>ければ<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>います。

examples.jp: 早く寝れば、朝元気になります。
examples.en: If you go to bed early, you'll feel good in the morning.
examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>れば、朝<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>になります。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The と-conditional expresses that one thing naturally or inevitably leads to another. It's used for natural laws, habitual consequences, and definite outcomes — 'when X happens, Y (always) happens'. It cannot be used with commands, requests, invitations, or volition in the main clause.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Dictionary form of verb (or plain non-past of adjective/copula) + と

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The main clause must be a natural/certain consequence. No commands/requests/invitations in the main clause.
Good for: natural laws, directions ('turn right and you'll see the bank'), habitual sequences.
Past tense usage expresses an unexpected discovery, similar to たら but with a nuance of automatic consequence.

examples.jp: このボタンを押すとドアが開きます。
examples.en: If you press this button, the door opens.
examples.furi: このボタンを<ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>すとドアが<ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 春になると桜が咲きます。
examples.en: When spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.furi: <ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>になると<ruby>桜<rt>さくら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>咲<rt>さ</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 右に曲がると、駅が見えます。
examples.en: If you turn right, you'll see the station.
examples.furi: <ruby>右<rt>みぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>曲<rt>ま</rt></ruby>がると、<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えます。

meaning: if (it is the case that) ___; as for ___

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: なら is a contextual conditional — 'if it's the case that X' — typically picking up on something already mentioned by the other speaker and responding to it. Unlike たら/ば/と, なら's main clause often comes temporally before the condition (i.e., the action in the main clause happens before the condition in time, when taken at face value). It is often used to give advice or recommendations based on what someone has just said.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form verb/adjective/noun + なら (drop だ for nouns and na-adjectives).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
No だ before なら for nouns: 学生なら (not 学生だなら).
Often used in advice-giving: 日本に行くなら、京都に行ってください ('if you're going to Japan, please visit Kyoto').
Distinct from のなら (or んなら) which emphasizes 'given that you're really planning to'.

examples.jp: 日本に行くなら、京都がおすすめです。
examples.en: If you're going to Japan, I recommend Kyoto.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くなら、<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>がおすすめです。

examples.jp: 寿司なら、あの店が一番です。
examples.en: When it comes to sushi, that shop is the best.
examples.furi: 寿司なら、あの<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>です。

examples.jp: 安いなら、買います。
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.furi: <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いなら、<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>います。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The plain volitional form is the casual counterpart of ましょう. It expresses 'let's do X' or 'I shall do X'. Combined with と思う, it expresses intention ('I'm thinking of doing X'). Combined with とする, it expresses an attempt ('to try to do X' or 'to be about to do X').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: drop る, add よう (食べる → 食べよう). Godan: u-row → o-row + う (行く → 行こう, 飲む → 飲もう). Irregular: する → しよう, くる → こよう.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Casual use: standalone as a suggestion ('let's eat!' — 食べよう!).
+ と思う: intention ('I'm thinking of going' — 行こうと思う).
+ とする: about to / attempt to ('I was about to leave' — 出ようとした).

examples.jp: 一緒に行こう。
examples.en: Let's go together. (casual)
examples.furi: <ruby>一緒<rt>いっしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>ぎょう</rt></ruby>こう。

examples.jp: 来年、日本へ行こうと思っています。
examples.en: I'm thinking of going to Japan next year.
examples.furi: <ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>ぎょう</rt></ruby>こうと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています。

examples.jp: そろそろ帰ろう。
examples.en: Let's head home soon. (casual)
examples.furi: そろそろ<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ろう。

point: Verb-て + はいけない / はいけません

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: てはいけない attaches the て-form of a verb to はいけない (polite: はいけません) to express prohibition — 'must not do X'. Casual speech often contracts it to ちゃいけない or ちゃだめ. It is used for rules, warnings, and firm prohibitions.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-て + はいけない (polite: はいけません). Casual contraction: ちゃいけない, ちゃだめ.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
ちゃ is a casual contraction of ては.
Alternative expressions: てはだめ (casual), てはなりません (very formal).
Opposite (permission): てもいい.

point: Verb-て + もいい / もいいです

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: てもいい attaches the て-form of a verb to もいい (polite: もいいです) to express permission or that something is acceptable — 'it's okay to do X', 'you may do X'. As a question, it asks for permission — 'may I do X?'. The more polite version is てもよろしい(ですか).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-て + もいい(です). More polite: てもよろしい(ですか).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
As a question: ～てもいいですか = 'may I ~?'.
てもかまいません ('I don't mind if ~') is another common polite form.
Opposite (prohibition): てはいけない.

examples.jp: ここに座ってもいいですか。

related: Verb-て + はいけない / はいけません

point: Verb-ない stem + なければならない

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: なければならない expresses necessity or obligation — 'must', 'have to'. It is formed from the ない-form of a verb by replacing the final い with ければならない. Many casual contractions exist: なきゃ(ならない), なくちゃ(いけない), ないといけない, etc. All of them express essentially the same meaning with varying levels of formality.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb-ない-stem (drop い from ない-form) + なければならない. Common casual forms: なきゃ, なくちゃ, ないと.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
ならない and いけない are interchangeable here; ならない is slightly more formal.
Casual 'must' forms: なきゃ (from なければ), なくちゃ (from なくては), ないと (trailing off but understood).
Opposite: なくてもいい ('don't have to').

meaning: don't have to / it's okay not to

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: なくてもいい expresses that something is unnecessary — 'don't have to', 'it's okay not to'. It is the negative counterpart of てもいい. The formation joins the negative stem of a verb (dropping the final い from ない-form) with the て-form construction.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Opposite: なければならない ('must').
Variant: なくてもかまわない ('I don't mind if you don't').

meaning: because / since ___ (softer, more objective than から)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ので expresses reason/cause similar to から, but with a softer, more objective, and often more polite feeling. It is preferred in formal requests and explanations where the speaker wants to avoid sounding pushy. The preceding clause is in plain form, but for noun and na-adjective predicates, なので is used instead of だので.

sections.html: Plain-form verb/い-adj + ので. Noun/な-adj + な + ので (学生なので, 静かなので).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
な is required for noun and na-adjective predicates: 学生なので, not 学生だので or 学生ので.
Often used in polite requests/explanations: 忙しいので、失礼します ('I'm busy so I'll excuse myself').

point: Clause + が / けど / けれども

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: が, けど, and けれども are conjunctions meaning 'but' or 'although'. They connect two clauses with a contrastive relationship. が is slightly more formal and written; けど is casual spoken; けれども is formal. They are also often used as soft sentence openers without a strong contrastive meaning — 'well…' or 'by the way…'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Clause (plain or polite) + が / けど / けれども + clause

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Formality ranking: けれども > が > けど (from more formal to less).
A common soft-opener use: すみませんが、道を教えてください ('excuse me, but could you tell me the way') — not really contrastive.
These are conjunctions, unlike しかし which is an adverb starting a new sentence.

related: Plain or polite form + から

point: Plain form + んです / のです
meaning: explains, gives reason, or softly asserts: 'it's that ___'

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: んです (more formal: のです) attaches to a plain-form clause to give an explanation, soften a statement, or provide context. It frames the statement as information the speaker is sharing in response to implicit or explicit questions or context. A classic use is explaining why something is happening: 頭が痛いんです ('(it's that) my head hurts' — used to explain absence or slow reaction). For nouns and な-adjectives, use なんです (学生なんです, not 学生だんです).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form verb/い-adj + んです. Noun/な-adj + な + んです (学生なんです).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For nouns and な-adjectives, insert な: 学生なんです.
In questions, んですか asks for explanation or clarification: なぜ来なかったんですか ('why didn't you come?').
More formal written form: のです.

related: Plain or polite form + から

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: なる means 'to become', expressing a natural or gradual change. For nouns and な-adjectives, the pattern is X + に + なる. For い-adjectives, drop い and add くなる (高い → 高くなる). The change is framed as happening on its own, as opposed to being caused by someone (for which use する).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun/な-adj + に + なる. い-adj: drop い, add くなる.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For caused change (making something become something), use に + する (部屋をきれいにする — 'make the room clean').
Common form ～ように なる: 'come to ___' (change in habit or ability).
Polite: なります; past: なった/なりました.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: にする expresses a decision or choice — 'I'll have X' in restaurants, 'I've decided on X' in general contexts. Literally it means 'make (it) into X' and is the active-voice counterpart to になる. It is the standard way to order food at a restaurant or make a selection.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + に + する

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Restaurant ordering: コーヒーにします ('I'll have coffee').

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 始める attached to a verb stem forms a compound expressing 'begin to do X'. It is an ichidan verb meaning 'to begin' in its own right, but also functions as an auxiliary when attached to another verb stem. Similar auxiliaries include 終わる ('finish'), 続ける ('continue'), 出す ('suddenly begin'), and others.

sections.html: Verb stem (same as ます stem) + 始める. E.g., 食べ始める ('begin to eat'), 読み始める ('begin to read').

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Uses the verb stem (connective form / -i form), which is the same stem as for ます.
Conjugates as an ichidan verb: 食べ始めた, 食べ始めます.
Related: 出す also means 'suddenly start' (泣き出す — 'burst into tears').

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 終わる attached to a verb stem forms a compound meaning 'finish doing X'. It is the completion counterpart to 始める. The standalone verb 終わる means 'to end' or 'to be over'. Note that 終える (transitive) can also be used: verb-stem + 終える.

sections.label: Usage

point: Verb stem / adj stem + すぎる

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: すぎる attaches to verb or adjective stems to mean 'too much' or 'overly'. For verbs, attach to the stem (食べる → 食べすぎる — 'eat too much'). For い-adjectives, drop the final い (高い → 高すぎる — 'too expensive'). For な-adjectives, attach directly to the stem (静かすぎる — 'too quiet'). The resulting verb conjugates as an ichidan verb.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb stem + すぎる. い-adj: drop い + すぎる. な-adj: + すぎる.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Exception: いい ('good') → よすぎる.
Conjugates as an ichidan verb: すぎます, すぎた, すぎない, etc.

sections.label: Usage

sections.html: Verb stem + にくい

sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: In Japanese, a full clause can modify a noun by being placed before it in plain form — there is no relative pronoun like 'which' or 'that'. For example, 昨日食べたケーキ literally 'yesterday-ate-cake' = 'the cake (that) I ate yesterday'. This is one of the most important structural differences from English and is essential for understanding longer sentences.

sections.html: Plain-form clause (including any subject marked with が rather than は) + Noun. For i-adjectives, the plain form directly precedes the noun (高い本 — 'an expensive book'). For na-adjectives, insert な (静かな部屋).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The modifying clause must be in plain form, not polite.
Within the modifying clause, the subject (if any) is usually marked with が, not は.
The head noun can be any syntactic role in the outer sentence (subject, object, etc.).

point: Verb-た + り + Verb-た + り + する
meaning: do things like X and Y (non-exhaustive list of actions)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜たり〜たりする lists actions non-exhaustively — 'do things like X and Y (among others)'. Unlike the sequential 〜て form, たり does not imply any particular order or timing; it just enumerates example actions. The final する carries the tense of the whole construction. A single たり is also grammatical ('do things like X'). The pattern is one of the most common N4 constructions and is essential for describing daily routines and varied activities.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-た form + り: 食べた → 食べたり, 飲んだ → 飲んだり. List actions with 〜たり〜たりする.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Non-exhaustive: implies 'among others' — these are examples, not a complete list.
Different from the sequential て-form, which orders actions in time.
A single たり + する is grammatical: 泣いたりした ('did things like cry').
For nouns / na-adjectives, the pattern is Nだったり: 暇だったり忙しかったり ('sometimes free, sometimes busy').

point: Transitive verb (他動詞) vs intransitive verb (自動詞) pairs
meaning: verb pairs distinguishing 'X does Y' (transitive) from 'Y happens' (intransitive)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: Japanese has many verb pairs where one form is transitive (an agent acts on something) and the other is intransitive (something happens on its own). The distinction is structural: transitive verbs take を for their object; intransitive verbs take が for the thing undergoing the action. Learning the pair patterns is essential to reading comprehension and to using the 〜ている / 〜てある state-of-affairs distinction correctly.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Common pairs (transitive / intransitive): 開ける/開く, 閉める/閉まる, 始める/始まる, 出す/出る, 入れる/入る, 上げる/上がる, 下げる/下がる, 見る/見える, 聞く/聞こえる, 消す/消える, 付ける/付く, 落とす/落ちる, 止める/止まる, 集める/集まる.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Transitive verb: 誰か が 何か を Verb (someone does something to something).
Intransitive verb: 何か が Verb (something happens to something).
Intransitive + 〜ている = resulting state from a natural change (ドアが開いている 'the door is open').
Transitive + 〜てある = resulting state from an intentional action (ドアが開けてある 'the door has been opened').
Not every Japanese verb has a pair; some stand alone.

examples.jp: ドアを開けました。
examples.en: I opened the door. (transitive)
examples.furi: ドアを<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けました。

examples.jp: ドアが開きました。
examples.en: The door opened. (intransitive)
examples.furi: ドアが<ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>きました。

examples.jp: 電気を消してください。
examples.en: Please turn off the light.
examples.furi: <ruby>電気<rt>でんき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>消<rt>け</rt></ruby>してください。

point: i-adj stem / 〜たい stem + がる
meaning: show signs of / appear to feel (third-person emotion)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜がる attaches to an adjective or a 〜たい form to express that a third person appears to feel a certain emotion, based on their observable behavior. Japanese treats one's own inner states (〜い, 〜たい) and the inner states of others differently: you can state your own feelings directly, but you must describe others' feelings as behaviorally observable — hence 〜がる ('show signs of being X'). Conjugates as a godan u-verb.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: i-adj: drop い, add がる: 寒い → 寒がる, 嬉しい → 嬉しがる, 痛い → 痛がる. 〜たい form: drop い, add がる: 食べたい → 食べたがる (see tagaru-third-person-desire).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Used for third-person observations: 彼は寒がっている ('he looks cold', inferred from his behavior).
Contrast: 私は寒い ('I am cold', direct) vs 彼は寒がっている (inferred).
Progressive form 〜がっている is most common for current observable state.
Conjugates as a regular godan -u verb: 寒がる, 寒がります, 寒がらない, 寒がった.

examples.jp: 弟は夏でも寒がる。
examples.en: My little brother gets cold even in summer.

related: Verb stem + たがる / たがっている
Noun + が + ほしい(です)

meaning: way of doing / how to do

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: V ます-stem + 方 (かた) forms a noun meaning 'way of doing X' or 'how to do X'. It is the core construction for describing methods and techniques. The object of the underlying verb takes の instead of を when modifying 方 — a surprising but consistent rule: 漢字の書き方 ('how to write kanji'), NOT 漢字を書き方. Indispensable for instructions, recipes, and teaching contexts.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V ます-stem + 方: 食べ方 ('way of eating'), 読み方 ('way of reading'), 使い方 ('way of using'). Irregular: する → し方 or やり方 (both used); for suru-compounds: 勉強のし方 (の inserted before し方).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The underlying verb's object takes の, not を, when attached to 方: 漢字の書き方.
Functions as a noun; can take particles, be a topic, be modified by adjectives.
Often used to ask 'how do I do X?': 〜方を教えてください ('please teach me how to ___').
やり方 is a common fixed form for 'way of doing' in general (not attached to a specific verb stem).

examples.jp: この漢字の書き方を教えてください。
examples.en: Please teach me how to write this kanji.
examples.furi: この<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>書<rt>しょ</rt></ruby>き<ruby>方<rt>ほう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてください。

examples.jp: 寿司の食べ方を知っていますか。
examples.en: Do you know how to eat sushi?
examples.furi: 寿司の<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ<ruby>方<rt>ほう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っていますか。

examples.en: Everyone has their own way of studying Japanese.

point: Verb plain non-past + ようにする / ようにしている
meaning: make it so that / try to do (habitually)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ようにする expresses making an effort to do something — either as a one-time decision ('I'll make sure to do X') or as an ongoing habit ('I try to do X'). The する form is the decision / resolve; the している form is the habitual effort. Negative 〜ないようにする means 'try not to do'. Distinct from ようになる ('come to be able to') and from ように-purpose ('in order to').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain non-past + ようにする (decision / resolve) or + ようにしている (ongoing habit). Negative: V ない + ようにする (try not to).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
する form: states a decision or resolution. している form: describes an ongoing habit.
Distinct from ようになる ('come to be able to') — that is a change-of-state construction.
Distinct from ように-purpose ('in order to') — that adverbially modifies a main-clause action.
Commonly used for lifestyle habits: 健康に気をつけるようにしている ('I try to be mindful of my health').

examples.jp: 毎日運動するようにしています。
examples.en: I make it a point to exercise every day.
examples.furi: <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>するようにしています。

examples.jp: 早く寝るようにします。
examples.en: I'll try to go to bed early.
examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るようにします。

related: V plain non-past (potential / intransitive / ない-form) + ように

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜てから expresses that the main-clause action happens after the 〜て form action is completed. It is sequential and emphasizes the 'after X' relationship between the two events. Distinct from the particle から ('because / from'), despite the shared から — here it is a compound with the て-form. Compare with 〜た後で, which more emphatically marks completion.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-て + から.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Sequential: the 〜てから action must be complete before the main clause begins.
Distinct from 〜た後で (more emphatic completion) and 〜前に (before).
Do not confuse with the particle から ('because / from') even though the characters are identical.
Common in instructions and routines: まず〜てから、そのあとに〜.

examples.jp: ご飯を食べてから、出かけます。
examples.en: I'll go out after eating.
examples.furi: ご<ruby>飯<rt>めし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べてから、<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけます。

examples.jp: 手を洗ってから、食べてください。
examples.en: Please eat after washing your hands.
examples.furi: <ruby>手<rt>て</rt></ruby>を<ruby>洗<rt>あら</rt></ruby>ってから、<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べてください。

examples.jp: 学校が終わってから、友達と遊びました。
examples.en: After school ended, I played with friends.
examples.furi: <ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わってから、<ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>と<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>びました。

related: V-た form / noun + の + 後で
V plain non-past / noun + の + 前に

point: V plain non-past / noun + の + 前に

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜前に marks a temporal 'before' clause. The verb in the 前に clause is ALWAYS in dictionary (plain non-past) form, regardless of whether the main clause describes a past, present, or future event — this is a common error point for learners who want to match tenses. For noun references, use noun + の + 前に.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain non-past + 前に (always dictionary form); noun + の + 前に.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Always use the dictionary (non-past) form of the verb in the 前に clause, even for past events.
For nouns: connect with の (会議の前に, not 会議前に for grammatical 'before').
Contrast with 〜た後で (uses past form); 〜前に is symmetrically non-past.
Without に, 前 alone is a noun meaning 'front / before'.

examples.jp: 寝る前に、歯を磨きます。
examples.en: Before going to bed, I brush my teeth.
examples.furi: <ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>歯<rt>は</rt></ruby>を<ruby>磨<rt>みが</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 食事の前に、手を洗ってください。
examples.en: Please wash your hands before the meal.
examples.furi: <ruby>食事<rt>しょくじ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>手<rt>て</rt></ruby>を<ruby>洗<rt>あら</rt></ruby>ってください。

examples.jp: 日本に来る前に、日本語を勉強しました。
examples.en: Before coming to Japan, I studied Japanese.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る<ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語を<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しました。

related: V-た form / noun + の + 後で

point: V-た form / noun + の + 後で

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜後で marks a temporal 'after' clause, using the past form of the verb (Vた) even when the main clause is in the future. More emphatic about the completion of the preceding action than 〜てから. For noun references, use noun + の + 後で.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-た + 後で; noun + の + 後で.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Verb must be in the past form (Vた) — the 前に / 後で symmetry is: 前に non-past, 後で past.
More completion-emphatic than 〜てから; both are valid but 〜後で feels more finished.
For nouns: use の (会議の後で, 仕事の後で).
The に / で distinction: 後 + に also exists (〜た後に) with similar meaning; 後で is more common in speech.

examples.jp: ご飯を食べた後で、散歩します。
examples.en: After eating, I'll take a walk.
examples.furi: ご<ruby>飯<rt>めし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた<ruby>後<rt>あと</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>します。

examples.jp: 学校の後で、図書館へ行きます。
examples.en: After school, I'll go to the library.
examples.furi: <ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>後<rt>あと</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 仕事が終わった後で、飲みに行きましょう。
examples.en: After work is over, let's go drinking.
examples.furi: <ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった<ruby>後<rt>あと</rt></ruby>で、<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きましょう。

related: V plain non-past / noun + の + 前に

point: V plain non-past + ことができる
meaning: can do / is able to do

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ことができる is an analytic way to express ability, equivalent to the potential form of the verb (食べられる). It is slightly more formal and more common in written Japanese, while the potential form dominates in speech. Both are fully grammatical and interchangeable in meaning, though the potential form is usually more concise. Negative: 〜ことができない.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain non-past + ことができる (polite: ことができます); negative: ことができない.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
More formal / written than the potential form, with identical meaning.
The potential form is more common in speech: 食べられる vs 食べることができる.
Noun version: noun + ができる ('can do X / X can be done'): 料理ができる ('can cook').
Chain with こと nominalization — builds on the more general こと nominalizer pattern.

examples.jp: 私は日本語を話すことができます。
examples.en: I can speak Japanese.
examples.furi: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語を<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>すことができます。

examples.jp: ここで泳ぐことができません。
examples.en: You cannot swim here.
examples.furi: ここで<ruby>泳<rt>およ</rt></ruby>ぐことができません。

examples.jp: 彼は料理することができる。
examples.en: He can cook.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>することができる。

related: Verb plain form / na-adj + な + こと

point: V plain non-past / V ない + ことにする

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ことにする expresses an active personal decision made by the speaker — 'I decided to do X'. Distinct from its passive counterpart 〜ことになる ('it has been decided'), where the decision comes from circumstance or others. The progressive form 〜ことにしている expresses a habitual decision or self-rule ('I make it a habit to'). Past form 〜ことにした = 'decided'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain non-past + ことにする (decide to); V ない + ことにする (decide not to); past: ことにした; progressive: ことにしている.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
〜ことにする vs 〜ことになる: する is the speaker's active decision; なる is the passive 'it was decided'.
Different from the noun-based ni-suru-decide (noun + にする 'decide on X from a menu of options').
Progressive ことにしている is the standard 'make it a habit' / 'make it a rule' form.
Common for lifestyle changes: 毎日運動することにした ('I decided to exercise every day').

examples.jp: 明日から毎日運動することにしました。
examples.en: I decided to exercise every day from tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>から<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>することにしました。

examples.jp: 甘いものを食べないことにしている。
examples.en: I've decided not to eat sweets (habitually).
examples.furi: <ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>いものを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べないことにしている。

examples.jp: 留学することにした。
examples.en: I decided to study abroad.
examples.furi: <ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>することにした。

related: V plain non-past / V ない + ことになる
Verb plain form / na-adj + な + こと

point: V plain non-past / V ない + ことになる
meaning: it is decided that / comes to be that

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ことになる expresses that a decision has been made by circumstance or others, without the speaker's direct agency — 'it was decided that X'. Its active counterpart is 〜ことにする ('I decided to do X'). The progressive form 〜ことになっている expresses an established rule, custom, or schedule. Past form 〜ことになった = 'it was (has been) decided'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain non-past + ことになる; V ない + ことになる; past: ことになった; progressive: ことになっている.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Passive counterpart of ことにする — the decision comes from outside the speaker.
〜ことになっている expresses social customs, rules, or regulations: 日本では〜することになっている.
Common in business and transfer announcements: 転勤することになりました ('it has been decided that I will transfer').
Different from ni-naru-become (noun → state change).

examples.jp: 来月、東京に転勤することになりました。
examples.en: It's been decided that I'll transfer to Tokyo next month.
examples.furi: <ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになりました。

examples.jp: 日本では靴を脱いで家に入ることになっている。
examples.en: In Japan, it's the rule to take off your shoes before entering a house.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>では<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>脱<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>いで<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ることになっている。

examples.jp: 会議は来週開くことになった。
examples.en: It's been decided that the meeting will be held next week.
examples.furi: <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>くことになった。

related: V plain non-past / V ない + ことにする
Verb plain form / na-adj + な + こと

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜なさい is a gentle command form, formed by adding なさい to the verb stem. It is less polite than 〜てください but not as abrupt as the bare imperative (食べろ). It is typical of parents to children, teachers to students, and written instructions ('answer the following' = 答えなさい). The form is too casual for polite adult-to-adult requests.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V ます-stem + なさい: 食べ → 食べなさい, 見 → 見なさい, 話し → 話しなさい. Irregular: する → しなさい, くる → きなさい.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Register: gentle command, appropriate in parent/teacher contexts or written instructions.
Too casual / condescending for polite adult-to-adult requests — use 〜てください instead.
Test/instruction writing: 次の問題に答えなさい ('answer the following questions').
The imperative form it softens: the bare godan imperative (食べろ) is much blunter.

examples.jp: 早く起きなさい。
examples.en: Wake up quickly!
examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きなさい。

examples.jp: 宿題をしなさい。
examples.en: Do your homework.
examples.furi: <ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>をしなさい。

examples.jp: 野菜を食べなさい。
examples.en: Eat your vegetables.
examples.furi: <ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べなさい。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜てほしい expresses the speaker's desire for another person to do something. The person being asked is typically marked with に. Distinct from 〜たい (own desire to do) and from ほしい alone (want a thing). The negative form 〜ないでほしい expresses 'want someone not to do X'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-て + ほしい; negative: V ないでほしい.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The person being asked takes に: 私に話してほしい ('I want you to talk to me').
Contrast: 〜たい (first-person own desire) vs 〜てほしい (desire that someone else act).
Negative: 〜ないでほしい ('don't do that, please').
Softer than 〜てください (request) — expresses desire rather than direct request.

examples.jp: 私の話を聞いてほしい。
examples.en: I want you to listen to me.
examples.furi: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いてほしい。

examples.jp: 手伝ってほしいです。
examples.en: I want (someone) to help me.
examples.furi: <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってほしいです。

examples.jp: 早く帰ってきてほしい。
examples.en: I want you to come home early.
examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ってきてほしい。

related: Noun + が + ほしい(です)

point: Plain form + し (+ plain form + し + ...)
meaning: and / besides (non-exhaustive listing of reasons or facts)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜し lists reasons or facts non-exhaustively — 'and moreover', 'for one thing'. The listed items are not the complete set; し implies there may be more. Often paired with a concluding clause that follows from the listed reasons. It is different from the sequential て-form in that it is for reasons/facts rather than actions in sequence.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form predicate + し; can chain multiple. Noun / na-adj + だ + し.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Non-exhaustive: implies there are more reasons than just those listed.
Often followed by から, a conclusion, or an implied consequence.
For noun/na-adj predicates, include だ: 便利だし, 学生だし.
Can stand alone at sentence end to trail off: 時間もないし... ('I don't have time, and...').

examples.jp: この部屋は広いし、静かだ。
examples.en: This room is spacious, and (also) quiet.
examples.furi: この<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>は<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>いし、<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かだ。

examples.jp: 時間もないし、お金もない。
examples.en: I have no time and no money.
examples.furi: <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>もないし、お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>もない。

meaning: I think I will / intend to do

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ようと思う combines the volitional (よう/おう) form with と思う ('think'), expressing the speaker's intention at the moment of speaking — 'I think I'll do X'. Less firm than 〜つもり (settled plan) but stronger than a vague wish. The progressive form 〜ようと思っている = 'have been thinking of'. For ichidan verbs use よう; for godan verbs use おう ending.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Ichidan: 食べる → 食べよう + と思う. Godan: 行く → 行こう + と思う. Irregular: する → しよう, くる → こよう.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
First-person intention at the moment of speaking; not as settled as つもり.
Progressive form 〜ようと思っている is common for 'have been thinking of'.
Builds on the standalone volitional form (see volitional-form) which expresses 'let's do' or solitary resolve.
Contrast with 〜たいと思う ('think I want to do') — しよう is about intention, したい is about desire.

meaning: (someone) does a favor for me / us

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜てくれる expresses that someone does something FOR the speaker or the speaker's in-group. The speaker benefits from the action. The honorific form 〜てくださる is used when the favor-giver is a superior. The giving-verb system (あげる / くれる / もらう) is central to Japanese expression of interpersonal kindness, and 〜てくれる captures the 'someone is kind to me' direction.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-て + くれる (polite: くれます); honorific: V-て + くださる (polite: くださいます).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The favor-giver takes が; the beneficiary (often 私 / us) is usually implied.
Part of the giving-verb trio: te-ageru (I do for others), te-kureru (others do for me), te-morau (I have someone do for me).
Honorific くださる: 先生が教えてくださった.
Negative くれない / くれなかった: 'didn't do the favor' — often with mild frustration.

meaning: I receive the favor of X doing Y / I have X do Y

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜てもらう expresses that the speaker or in-group receives the benefit of another's action — 'I have someone do X for me'. The person performing the action takes に. The humble form 〜ていただく is used when the other party is a superior. Common as a polite request: 〜てもらえますか ('could you...?').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Subject (recipient) は/が + Agent に + V-て + もらう.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The agent (performer) takes に: 友達に手伝ってもらった ('had my friend help').
Request forms: 〜てもらえますか (polite), 〜てもらえる (plain), 〜ていただけますか (very polite).
Humble form 〜ていただく is essential in business and formal contexts.
Contrast with 〜てくれる: くれる focuses on the giver's action; もらう focuses on the recipient's receipt.

meaning: I do a favor for (someone outside my in-group)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜てあげる expresses that the speaker does something FOR someone else, usually outside the speaker's close in-group. The recipient takes に. A usage caution: saying 〜てあげる directly to the hearer can sound condescending, because it draws attention to the favor. Humble form さしあげる is used for superiors.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-て + あげる (polite: あげます); humble: V-て + さしあげる (polite: さしあげます).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The recipient takes に: 友達に本を貸してあげる.
CAUTION: saying 'I'll ~てあげる' directly to someone can sound condescending; often softened in practice.
Humble さしあげる: 先生に手紙を書いてさしあげる — use for superiors, but sparingly (it can sound overly formal).
Part of the giving-verb trio (あげる / くれる / もらう).

meaning: to give (outward, from in-group to out-group)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: あげる is the basic verb for 'give', used when the giver is the speaker or in-group and the receiver is outside that group. Crucially, do NOT use あげる when giving TO yourself (use くれる in that direction), and do NOT use あげる for superiors (use さしあげる or reformulate). The full giving-verb system is: あげる (outward), くれる (toward speaker), もらう (receive).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain verb あげる (polite: あげます). Particles: Giver が / は, Receiver に, Object を.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Do NOT use あげる for gifts TO you — use くれる instead.
Do NOT use あげる for gifts to clearly superior persons — use さしあげる (humble) or paraphrase.
Direction matters: あげる = outward (from in-group to out-group), くれる = toward speaker.
Basic verb meaning 'give' — the foundation for the 〜てあげる auxiliary.

point: Giver が (Receiver に) Object を くれる

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: くれる is the verb 'give' used when the giver is someone else and the receiver is the speaker or in-group. The receiver (often 私) is commonly implied and omitted. The honorific form くださる is used when the giver is a superior. Parallel to あげる (outward direction) but from the opposite perspective.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain verb くれる (polite: くれます); honorific: くださる (polite: くださいます — irregular, note the final います not りまする).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The receiver (typically 私 or in-group) can be implied and often is dropped from the sentence.
Honorific くださる — used when the giver is a superior (先生がくださった).
Note the irregular honorific polite form くださいます (not くださります).
Basic verb meaning 'give toward me/us' — the foundation for the 〜てくれる auxiliary.

point: Receiver が Giver に / から Object を もらう

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: もらう is the verb 'receive', used from the receiver's perspective in a giving transaction. The giver takes に or から; the receiver is the subject. Humble form いただく is used when receiving from superiors. Together with あげる and くれる, もらう completes the Japanese giving-verb system — each verb takes a different perspective on the same kind of event.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain verb もらう (polite: もらいます); humble: いただく (polite: いただきます).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Giver particle: に or から (both grammatical; から is common when the giver is distant).
Humble form いただく — used when receiving from a superior or in formal contexts.
The polite form いただきます is also the pre-meal greeting — same word, same root idea.
Basic verb meaning 'receive' — the foundation for the 〜てもらう auxiliary.

point: お + V ます-stem + ください (or ご + Sino-Japanese noun + ください)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: お〜ください is a very polite honorific request form, more formal than 〜てください. It is the form used in customer service announcements, public signage, and formal instructions. For native Japanese verbs, use お + ます-stem; for Sino-Japanese nouns ('suru' verbs), use ご + noun. Some verbs have fixed honorific forms that replace this pattern (e.g., 来る → お越しください).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: お + V ます-stem + ください (native verbs): お待ちください, お座りください. ご + Sino-Japanese noun + ください: ご注意ください, ご利用ください.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Very polite — typical of customer service, public announcements, formal instructions.
The お vs ご distinction tracks native vs Sino-Japanese: native verbs take お; Sino-Japanese nouns take ご.
Not all verbs work with this pattern — some have dedicated honorific forms (来る → お越しください, 見る → ご覧ください).
More formal than the basic 〜てください.

meaning: honorific use of passive form (polite way to describe superior's actions)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: The 〜れる / 〜られる form (normally the passive) is also used as an honorific (尊敬語), describing the actions of a superior politely. The conjugation is identical to the passive; context determines whether it is passive or honorific — usually clear from the subject (a superior) and the non-patient nature of the action. Less formal than dedicated honorific verbs (いらっしゃる, ご覧になる) but common in business speech.

sections.label: Formation

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:

Context disambiguates: a subject who is a superior performing their own (non-victim) action implies honorific.
Less formal than お〜になる or dedicated honorific verbs (いらっしゃる, なさる, おっしゃる).
Common in business and polite speech; easier to use than the full honorific vocabulary.

point: お + V ます-stem + する (or ご + Sino-Japanese noun + する)
meaning: humble form: I will do X (for a superior)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: お〜する is the 謙譲語 (humble) form for the speaker's own actions when speaking to or about a superior. It lowers the speaker to elevate the listener. Like the honorific お〜ください, the お vs ご distinction tracks native vs Sino-Japanese roots. Common in business contexts for everyday actions — 'I'll call you', 'I'll explain'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: お + V ます-stem + する (native verbs): お貸しする, お書きする. ご + Sino-Japanese noun + する: ご案内する, ご説明する.

sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Emphasizes humility — the speaker is performing the action for a superior.
お vs ご: お for native verbs, ご for Sino-Japanese nouns.
Polite form: お〜します / ご〜します.
Common in business: お願いします, ご案内します.

More casual than のような-based equivalents (このような etc.).

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜たいと思う softens the direct 〜たい by framing it as something the speaker 'thinks'. Literally 'think I want to do X', functionally 'I'd like to do X'. Less direct and more polite than bare 〜たい. The progressive form 〜たいと思っている expresses a sustained wish ('I've been wanting to'). sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:

Progressive form 〜たいと思っている: 'have been wanting to do X'.

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜場合 introduces a hypothetical scenario or specific case — 'in the event that X'. sections.html: V plain + 場合; i-adj + 場合; na-adj + な + 場合; noun + の + 場合.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:

Often appears in warnings and emergency signage: 火事の場合, 遅れる場合.
The optional は (〜場合は) marks the case as a topic for contrast.

meaning: each / per / at a rate of

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ずつ attaches to a number + counter to express distribution — 'X each', 'X per unit', 'X at a time'. Common for fair distribution ('one each'), gradual progress ('little by little'), and instructing groups. Functions adverbially, modifying a verb or action.

sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Distributive sense: each person/unit gets the quantity.
Gradual-progress sense: 少しずつ ('little by little'), 一歩ずつ ('step by step').
Works with any counter, including indefinite 少し ('little').
Adverbial in function — modifies the main verb.

examples.jp: 一つずつ取ってください。
examples.en: Please take one each.
examples.furi: <ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つずつ<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>ってください。

examples.jp: 少しずつ食べます。
examples.en: I eat (it) little by little.
examples.furi: <ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しずつ<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べます。

examples.jp: 二人ずつ並んでください。
examples.en: Please line up in pairs (two each).
examples.furi: <ruby>二人<rt>ふたり</rt></ruby>ずつ<ruby>並<rt>なら</rt></ruby>んでください。

point: V plain non-past + つもりだった
meaning: had intended to / was going to

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜つもりだった is the past form of つもり (intention), expressing an intention held at a past moment — 'I had intended to do X'. Often implies the intention was NOT carried out, with an adversative follow-up ('I was going to, but...'). Distinct from 〜たつもり, which means 'thought I did X' (mistaken belief about having done something).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain non-past + つもりだった / つもりでした.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Past form of つもり — the intention is placed in the past, regardless of whether it was carried out.
Often implies non-realization: 〜つもりだったけど、〜 ('was going to, but...').
Distinct from 〜たつもり, which uses the past verb form + つもり and means 'thought I did' (usually a mistaken belief).
Common for retrospection and apology.

examples.jp: 昨日、勉強するつもりだったけど、疲れて寝てしまった。
examples.en: I was going to study yesterday, but I was tired and fell asleep.
examples.furi: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>するつもりだったけど、<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れて<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てしまった。

examples.jp: 来るつもりでしたが、都合が悪くなりました。
examples.en: I was planning to come, but something came up.
examples.furi: <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るつもりでしたが、<ruby>都合<rt>つごう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>悪<rt>あく</rt></ruby>くなりました。

examples.jp: 朝ごはんを食べるつもりだった。
examples.en: I had intended to eat breakfast.
examples.furi: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べるつもりだった。

point: V plain / i-adj / noun の / na-adj な + はずだった
meaning: was supposed to / should have been

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜はずだった is the past form of はず (expectation), expressing that an outcome was expected but did NOT occur. Often implies surprise, disappointment, or contradiction with reality. Commonly paired with のに or が/けど for the unexpected reality clause. Distinct from はずがない ('there's no way').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V plain + はずだった; i-adj + はずだった; noun + の + はずだった; na-adj + な + はずだった.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Expresses an unrealized expectation — the expected outcome did not happen.
Often paired with のに or が for the contrary reality: 今日来るはずだったのに、来なかった.
Contrasted with the present はず (ordinary expectation).
Can also express 'should have been' without explicit contradiction, depending on context.

examples.jp: 彼は今日来るはずだった。
examples.en: He was supposed to come today.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るはずだった。

examples.jp: 試験は簡単なはずだった。
examples.en: The exam was supposed to be easy.
examples.furi: <ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>簡単<rt>かんたん</rt></ruby>なはずだった。

examples.jp: 昨日、雨が降るはずでしたが、晴れました。
examples.en: It was supposed to rain yesterday, but it was sunny.
examples.furi: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>るはずでしたが、<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れました。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: Noun + でも has two related senses: (1) 'even (a) X' — expressing that even unlikely cases apply ('even a child can do it'); (2) 'or something / or the like' — used for non-specific casual suggestions ('how about tea or something?'). Distinct from sentence-initial でも ('however / but') which is a conjunction.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + でも.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Sense 1 (even a): 子供でもわかる, 忙しくても, etc.
Sense 2 (or something): お茶でも飲みませんか — non-specific casual suggestion, common in invitations.
Not the same as sentence-initial でも ('but / however'), which is a conjunction.
Also combines with pronouns: 誰でも ('anyone'), どこでも ('anywhere'), いつでも ('any time').

examples.jp: 子供でもわかる。
examples.en: Even a child can understand.
examples.furi: <ruby>子供<rt>こども</rt></ruby>でもわかる。

examples.jp: 雨でも行きます。
examples.en: I'll go even if it rains.
examples.furi: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: お茶でもどうですか。
examples.en: How about some tea (or something)?
examples.furi: お<ruby>茶<rt>ちゃ</rt></ruby>でもどうですか。

related: Verb-て + もいい / もいいです

meaning: I humbly receive the favor of X doing Y (humble)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ていただく is the humble-form version of 〜てもらう, used when the favor-doer is a superior or in formal contexts. It is essential in business and polite Japanese. The request form 〜ていただけますか ('could you kindly do X?') is very commonly used in customer service, formal requests, and polite inquiries — it is widely considered one of the softest/most polite ways to ask for something.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-て + いただく (polite: いただきます). Request form: 〜ていただけますか / 〜ていただけませんか.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Humble version of 〜てもらう — the speaker is receiving from a superior.
Request form 〜ていただけますか is one of the softest ways to ask for something in polite Japanese.
〜ていただけませんか is slightly softer still (literally 'won't you kindly?').
Common in business, customer service, and formal writing.

examples.jp: 先生に説明していただきました。
examples.en: I had my teacher explain it (to me).
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>していただきました。

examples.jp: 少し待っていただけますか。
examples.en: Could you kindly wait a moment?
examples.furi: <ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていただけますか。

examples.jp: 教えていただいて、ありがとうございました。
examples.en: Thank you for kindly teaching me.
examples.furi: <ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えていただいて、ありがとうございました。

meaning: should / just need to / it'd be good if

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ばいい expresses advice or a sufficient condition — 'you just need to do X' or 'it would be good if X'. The question form どうすればいい is an extremely common way to ask 'what should I do?'. Softer and more suggestion-like than 〜べきだ (moral should). Distinct from 〜ばよかった, which is the past form expressing regret about an unrealized past action.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V ば-form + いい / いいです. Question: どうすればいい(ですか).

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Expresses a sufficient/minimally-required action rather than a strong obligation.
Question form どうすればいい / どうすればいいですか — extremely common 'what should I do?'.
Contrast with 〜ばよかった (regret over past non-action, N3).
Softer than 〜べきだ (moral should, N3).

examples.jp: 分からなかったら、聞けばいいです。
examples.en: If you don't understand, you can just ask.
examples.furi: <ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からなかったら、<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>けばいいです。

examples.jp: どうすればいいですか。
examples.en: What should I do?
examples.furi: どうすればいいですか。

examples.jp: 早く寝ればいい。
examples.en: You just need to go to bed early.
examples.furi: <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ればいい。

point: Giver が Receiver に Object を やる
meaning: to give (casual / to inferiors, pets, plants)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: やる is the casual, down-ward variant of あげる — used when giving to someone or something distinctly below the speaker's social position, such as pets, plants, younger siblings, or in rough masculine speech. It can sound rude if used inappropriately. The 〜てやる auxiliary form is also very common in casual male speech as a rougher equivalent of 〜てあげる ('I'll do it for you', sometimes with threatening or dismissive tone).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain verb やる (polite やります). Particles: Giver が, Receiver に, Object を.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Used mainly for pets, plants, and younger in-group members. Can sound rude to equals or superiors.
The 〜てやる auxiliary has a masculine / rough edge; 〜てあげる is the neutral default.
Also means 'to do' in other contexts (宿題をやる 'do homework') — a distinct sense of the same verb.
Between close friends, やる may be used casually without negative nuance.

examples.jp: 毎朝、花に水をやります。
examples.en: Every morning I water the flowers.
examples.furi: <ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>花<rt>はな</rt></ruby>に<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>をやります。

examples.jp: 犬にえさをやった。
examples.en: I fed the dog.
examples.furi: <ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>にえさをやった。

examples.jp: 弟に宿題を手伝ってやった。
examples.en: I helped my little brother with his homework.
examples.furi: <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってやった。

meaning: even if / even though (hypothetical or counterfactual contrast)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ても is a hypothetical concessive — 'even if X, (still) Y'. It expresses that the main clause holds regardless of the 〜ても clause. Distinct from the related 〜てもいい (permission — covered separately as te-mo-ii-permission) in that the meaning here is concessive, not permissive. Commonly paired with interrogatives or emphatic words: いくら〜ても ('no matter how much'), どんなに〜ても ('no matter how').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V-て + も; i-adj drop い + くても (高くても); na-adj / noun + でも.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Different from 〜てもいい (permission) — same structure, different function.
Often combined with emphatics: いくら〜ても, どんなに〜ても, どこに行っても.
The noun/na-adj form 〜でも coincides with the 'even a N' / 'or something' sense (see demo-noun-even).
Can chain with other concessive markers for emphasis.

examples.jp: 雨が降っても、行きます。
examples.en: I'll go even if it rains.
examples.furi: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>お</rt></ruby>っても、<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。

examples.jp: 高くても買う。

examples.jp: いくら食べても太らない。
examples.en: No matter how much I eat, I don't gain weight.
examples.furi: いくら<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べても<ruby>太<rt>ふと</rt></ruby>らない。

point: いらっしゃる (honorific of 行く / 来る / いる)
meaning: (honorific) to go / to come / to be (at a place)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: いらっしゃる is a dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb that replaces all three of 行く (go), 来る (come), and いる (be at a place) when describing a superior's actions politely. It conjugates as a godan verb with one irregularity: the polite form is いらっしゃいます (not いらっしゃります). Common in customer service: いらっしゃいませ ('welcome' — literally 'please come/be').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: いらっしゃる. Polite: いらっしゃいます (note irregular — い dropped before ます). Te-form: いらっしゃって. Imperative: いらっしゃい.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
One verb covers three meanings — context disambiguates.
Polite form is IRREGULAR: ます-stem uses いらっしゃい (not the expected いらっしゃり), so polite is いらっしゃいます.
Fixed phrase いらっしゃいませ is used by shops to welcome customers.
Also used as a polite greeting: 先生、いらっしゃいますか — 'Is the teacher in?'

examples.jp: 先生は今、学校にいらっしゃいます。
examples.en: The teacher is at the school now.
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>にいらっしゃいます。

examples.jp: 明日、お客様がいらっしゃいます。
examples.en: A guest will come tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、お客様がいらっしゃいます。

examples.jp: いらっしゃいませ。
examples.en: Welcome. (shop greeting)
examples.furi: いらっしゃいませ。

point: おっしゃる (honorific of 言う)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: おっしゃる is the dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb replacing 言う when describing a superior's speech politely. Like いらっしゃる, it has an irregular polite form: おっしゃいます (not おっしゃります). Common in business phrases like 'what did you say?' (何とおっしゃいましたか) and 'as you say' (おっしゃる通り).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: おっしゃる. Polite: おっしゃいます (irregular — い drop before ます). Te-form: おっしゃって.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Polite form is IRREGULAR: おっしゃいます, not おっしゃります.
Common fixed phrase: おっしゃる通り ('just as you say / exactly as you said').
Used only for others' speech, never the speaker's own (use 申す for humble own-speech).
In business, the noun-like construction お名前は何とおっしゃいますか is a polite way to ask 'what is your name?'.

examples.jp: 先生は何とおっしゃいましたか。
examples.en: What did the teacher say?
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>とおっしゃいましたか。

examples.jp: お客様がそうおっしゃいました。
examples.en: The customer said so.
examples.furi: お客様がそうおっしゃいました。

examples.jp: おっしゃる通りです。
examples.en: It's just as you say.
examples.furi: おっしゃる<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>りです。

point: ご覧になる (honorific of 見る)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: ご覧になる is the dedicated honorific form of 見る ('see / look at / watch'). It conjugates as a regular godan verb (ご覧になります, ご覧になって). The shortened form ご覧ください ('please look') appears frequently on signs, in announcements, and in instructions. Distinct from the simple honorific 見られる, which is the passive-as-honorific construction applied to 見る.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Base form: ご覧になる. Polite: ご覧になります. Request: ご覧ください ('please look'). Te-form: ご覧になって.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
More formally polite than the passive-as-honorific 見られる.
ご覧ください is the most common way to say 'please look' in announcements and signage.
Used only for others' viewing, never the speaker's own (use 拝見する 拝見いたします for humble own-viewing).
Common in TV/media: あちらをご覧ください ('please look over there').

examples.jp: こちらの資料をご覧ください。
examples.en: Please look at this document.
examples.furi: こちらの<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>をご覧ください。

examples.jp: 先生はもうその映画をご覧になりましたか。
examples.en: Has the teacher already seen that movie?
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>はもうその<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>をご覧になりましたか。

examples.jp: 画面をご覧になりながらお聞きください。
examples.en: Please listen while looking at the screen.
examples.furi: <ruby>画面<rt>がめん</rt></ruby>をご覧になりながらお<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>きください。

related: お + V ます-stem + ください (or ご + Sino-Japanese noun + ください)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: なさる is the dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb replacing する when describing a superior's actions politely. Like the other irregular honorific verbs, it has an irregular polite form: なさいます (not なさります). Common with suru-compounds: 勉強なさる, 説明なさる. The request form なさってください is a polite way to say 'please do X', though お〜ください is more common for simple requests.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: なさる. Polite: なさいます (irregular). Te-form: なさって. Request: なさってください.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Polite form IRREGULAR: なさいます, not なさります.
Extends to suru-compounds: 勉強なさる, 心配なさる, 連絡なさる.
Used only for others' actions. For the speaker's own actions, use いたす (humble of する).
The imperative なさい (used by parents / teachers) comes from this verb but is not itself honorific — it is a gentle command.

examples.jp: 社長は毎朝運動をなさいます。
examples.en: The company president exercises every morning.
examples.furi: <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>をなさいます。

examples.jp: お客様は何をなさいますか。
examples.en: What would you like to do, sir/madam?
examples.furi: お客様は<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>をなさいますか。

examples.jp: お気をつけてお帰りなさい。
examples.en: Please take care on your way home.
examples.furi: お<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>をつけてお<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りなさい。

point: 参る (humble of 行く / 来る)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 参る is the dedicated humble (謙譲語) verb replacing both 行く and 来る when describing the speaker's own movement politely, especially toward a superior or in formal contexts. Conjugates as a regular godan verb. Common in formal announcements: 'the train is coming' (電車が参ります), and in polite business phrases: 'I'll be right there' (すぐ参ります).

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: 参る. Polite: 参ります. Te-form: 参って.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Humble (謙譲語) — used for the speaker's own actions to elevate the listener.
Covers both 'go' and 'come' — context disambiguates.
Also appears in train/station announcements: まもなく電車が参ります ('the train is arriving soon') — here the humble register is used to polite address to passengers.
Common in business: 後ほど参ります ('I'll come later').

examples.jp: すぐ参ります。
examples.en: I'll come right away.
examples.furi: すぐ<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります。

examples.jp: 東京から参りました。
examples.en: I came from Tokyo.
examples.furi: <ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>から<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>りました。

examples.jp: まもなく電車が参ります。
examples.en: The train is arriving shortly.
examples.furi: まもなく<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります。

meaning: (humble) to say / to be called (a name)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 申す is the dedicated humble (謙譲語) verb replacing 言う for the speaker's own speech in polite contexts. The most common use is in self-introductions: 'I'm called X' (Xと申します). The more formal 申し上げる adds extra humility (お礼を申し上げます — 'I express my thanks'). Business and formal speech rely heavily on this verb.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: 申す. Polite: 申します. More formal: 申し上げる / 申し上げます.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Humble (謙譲語) — for the speaker's own speech toward a superior or in formal contexts.
Self-introduction formula: 〜と申します ('I am called / my name is ~').
More formal 申し上げる is used for gratitude and formal acknowledgment.
Never used for others' speech — use おっしゃる (honorific) instead.

examples.jp: 田中と申します。
examples.en: My name is Tanaka. (humble self-introduction)
examples.furi: 田中と<ruby>申<rt>さる</rt></ruby>します。

examples.jp: 心よりお礼を申し上げます。
examples.en: I express my gratitude from the heart.
examples.furi: <ruby>心<rt>こころ</rt></ruby>よりお<ruby>礼<rt>れい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げます。

examples.jp: 先ほど申した通りです。
examples.en: It's just as I said earlier.
examples.furi: <ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>申<rt>さる</rt></ruby>した<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>りです。
