おっしゃる (honorific of 言う)

point: いただく (humble of もらう / 食べる / 飲む)
meaning: (humble) to receive / to eat / to drink

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: いただく is the humble (謙譲語) verb that covers three closely related meanings: (1) to receive, as humble of もらう; (2) to eat, as humble of 食べる; (3) to drink, as humble of 飲む. The pre-meal greeting いただきます comes from sense (2) — literally 'I humbly receive / eat'. The polite form いただきます is by far the most common form. See also the auxiliary 〜ていただく covered separately.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: いただく. Polite: いただきます.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Three meanings share the same verb: receive, eat, drink.
Pre-meal greeting いただきます is the most common usage — formally humble, functionally routine.
Also used in business: 資料をいただきました ('I received the documents').
The auxiliary 〜ていただく (humble of 〜てもらう) is covered separately as te-itadaku-polite-favor-received.

examples.jp: いただきます。
examples.en: I humbly receive (this meal). (pre-meal greeting)
examples.furi: いただきます。

examples.jp: お手紙をいただきました。
examples.en: I received your letter. (humble)
examples.furi: お<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>をいただきました。

examples.jp: お茶をいただけますか。
examples.en: May I have some tea?
examples.furi: お<ruby>茶<rt>ちゃ</rt></ruby>をいただけますか。

related: Receiver が Giver に / から Object を もらう

point: くださる (honorific of くれる)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: くださる is the dedicated honorific (尊敬語) verb replacing くれる when the giver is a superior. Like other irregular honorific verbs, its polite form is irregular: くださいます (not くださります). The imperative ください ('please') is derived from this verb and is extremely common. The auxiliary 〜てくださる (honorific of 〜てくれる) describes a superior doing a favor for the speaker.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain: くださる. Polite: くださいます (irregular). Imperative: ください.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Polite form IRREGULAR: くださいます, not くださります.
The imperative ください — used as 'please' — is the most common form and is derived from this verb.
〜てくださる auxiliary: honorific of 〜てくれる (a superior does a favor toward the speaker).
Used only when the giver is a superior; use くれる for neutral in-group giving.

examples.jp: 先生が本をくださいました。
examples.en: The teacher kindly gave me a book.
examples.furi: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>をくださいました。

examples.jp: 社長がお花をくださった。
examples.en: The president (kindly) gave me flowers.
examples.furi: <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>がお<ruby>花<rt>はな</rt></ruby>をくださった。

examples.jp: お手紙をくださってありがとうございます。
examples.en: Thank you for kindly sending me a letter.
examples.furi: お<ruby>手紙<rt>てがみ</rt></ruby>をくださってありがとうございます。

related: Giver が (Receiver に) Object を くれる

point: Noun (or V plain) + しか + negative predicate

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: しか is a negative-polarity 'only' marker: it must be paired with a negative predicate to give a 'only X' meaning. It is more emphatic and more restrictive than だけ, often carrying a sense of 'only this (and nothing else)' or 'no more than X'. The main clause MUST be in the negative form even though the meaning in English is positive ('only').

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + しか + ない / いません (negative); V plain (often potential) + しか + ない / いません.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Requires a NEGATIVE main clause — English speakers often forget this.
More emphatic / restrictive than だけ: 100円しかない ('I have only 100 yen (and no more)') vs 100円だけある ('I have just 100 yen').
Commonly attached after quantities to emphasize insufficiency: 一つしかない ('there's only one').
Can follow other particles: からしか, までしか, でしか.

examples.jp: お金が100円しかない。
examples.en: I only have 100 yen.
examples.furi: お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>が100円しかない。

examples.jp: 日本語しか話せません。
examples.en: I can only speak Japanese.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語しか<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>せません。

examples.jp: 一つしか残っていない。
examples.en: There's only one left.
examples.furi: <ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つしか<ruby>残<rt>のこ</rt></ruby>っていない。

related: Noun / verb (〜て form / plain) + ばかり

point: Noun + が + 好き / 嫌い
meaning: like / dislike (object takes が, not を)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: In Japanese, the objects of 好き ('like') and 嫌い ('dislike') are marked with が, NOT を. This is because 好き / 嫌い are na-adjectives describing the subject's state, not transitive verbs. The full structure is [subject は / が] [object が] 好き/嫌い. 大好き ('love') and 大嫌い ('hate') are the emphatic forms.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: (Subject は) + Object が + 好き / 嫌い / 大好き / 大嫌い + です / だ.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The object takes が, NOT を — 好き and 嫌い are na-adjectives, not verbs.
大好き ('very much like / love') and 大嫌い ('very much dislike / hate') are standard emphatic forms.
Negatives: 好きじゃない / 嫌いじゃない.
Parallel to other が-marking predicates like わかる and できる.

examples.jp: 私は猫が好きです。
examples.en: I like cats.
examples.furi: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。

examples.jp: 彼は納豆が嫌いだ。
examples.en: He dislikes natto.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>納豆<rt>なっとう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>嫌<rt>きら</rt></ruby>いだ。

examples.jp: 日本語の勉強が大好きです。
examples.en: I love studying Japanese.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語の<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大好<rt>だいす</rt></ruby>きです。

meaning: understand (object takes が, not を)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: わかる ('understand / know / be clear') takes its object with が, NOT を. This is because わかる is syntactically intransitive — 'X は Y が わかる' literally means 'as for X, Y is understandable'. The same が-marking applies to できる, 好き / 嫌い, 見える, and 聞こえる. Note that わかる is distinct from 知る ('know (a fact)'), which DOES take を.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: (Subject は) + Object が + わかる / わかります. Negative: わからない / わかりません.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The understood thing takes が, NOT を.
Contrast with 知る ('know a fact'), which is transitive and takes を (日本語を知っている 'I know Japanese').
わかる vs 知っている: わかる is about understanding / grasping; 知っている is about having factual knowledge.
Common: 日本語がわかる ('I understand Japanese'), 意味がわからない ('I don't understand the meaning').

examples.jp: 日本語がわかります。
examples.en: I understand Japanese.
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語がわかります。

examples.jp: 彼の気持ちがわからない。
examples.en: I don't understand his feelings.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>あ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気持<rt>きも</rt></ruby>ちがわからない。

examples.jp: この問題が全然わかりません。
examples.en: I don't understand this problem at all.
examples.furi: この<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>全然<rt>ぜんぜん</rt></ruby>わかりません。

related: Noun + が + 好き / 嫌い

meaning: can do / is possible (object takes が, not を)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: できる is the 'can do' verb that takes its object with が, not を. It can express (1) ability to do X (日本語ができる 'can do (speak) Japanese'), (2) the completion / creation of something (ご飯ができた 'the meal is ready'), or (3) possibility. It is the potential form of する and can always be substituted for the より-explicit 〜することができる pattern.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: (Subject は) + Object が + できる / できます. Negative: できない / できません.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Object takes が, NOT を — unlike the verbs it can substitute for.
Also serves as the potential form of する: 勉強する → 勉強できる.
Second sense: 'be completed / be ready' (ご飯ができた 'the meal is ready', 子供ができた 'I'm pregnant / a child has been born').
Equivalent to the longer 〜することができる in most contexts.

examples.jp: 日本語ができますか。
examples.en: Can you speak Japanese?
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語ができますか。

examples.jp: ご飯ができました。
examples.en: The meal is ready.
examples.furi: ご<ruby>飯<rt>めし</rt></ruby>ができました。

examples.jp: 運転ができる。
examples.en: I can drive.
examples.furi: <ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>ができる。

related: V plain non-past + ことができる
Noun + が + 好き / 嫌い

point: Noun + が + 聞こえる / 見える
meaning: is audible / is visible (spontaneous perception; object takes が)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 聞こえる ('be audible / can be heard') and 見える ('be visible / can be seen') express spontaneous perception — something reaches the observer without active effort. They take their object (the audible / visible thing) with が. Distinct from the potential forms 聞ける / 見られる, which express ability (the ability to hear/see something). Roughly: 聞こえる = 'I can hear it (it's loud enough)'; 聞ける = 'I have the ability to hear it (e.g., my ears work)'.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: (Subject には) + Object が + 聞こえる / 見える.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Spontaneous perception — the sound or sight reaches you without effort.
Contrast with potential: 聞こえる (spontaneous 'is audible') vs 聞ける (potential 'can hear').
Contrast: 見える (spontaneous 'is visible') vs 見られる (potential 'can see / can watch').
The perceiver can be marked with には: 私には音楽が聞こえる ('to me, music is audible').

examples.jp: 遠くから音楽が聞こえる。
examples.en: I can hear music from far away.
examples.furi: <ruby>遠<rt>とお</rt></ruby>くから<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえる。

examples.jp: ここから富士山が見えます。
examples.en: You can see Mount Fuji from here.
examples.furi: ここから富士山が<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えます。

examples.jp: 小さい声が聞こえない。
examples.en: I can't hear the quiet voice.
examples.furi: <ruby>小<rt>ちい</rt></ruby>さい<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえない。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: だから as a sentence-initial conjunction means 'so / therefore / that's why', linking a previous statement (reason) to the current statement (conclusion). It is the standalone / sentence-initial version of the causal から. In casual speech, it can sometimes imply 'that's what I'm saying' or a slight frustration. The polite equivalent is ですから.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: [Previous sentence]. だから [current sentence].

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Sentence-initial conjunction, different from the particle から ('because / from').
Polite equivalent: ですから.
Casual tone; in frustrated speech can mean 'that's what I've been saying!'
More formal alternatives: したがって, ゆえに (written).

examples.jp: 雨が降っています。だから、傘を持っていきます。
examples.en: It's raining. So I'll take an umbrella.
examples.furi: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>お</rt></ruby>っています。だから、<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っていきます。

examples.jp: 疲れました。だから、今日は早く寝ます。
examples.en: I'm tired. So I'll go to bed early today.
examples.furi: <ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れました。だから、<ruby>今日<rt>こんにち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ます。

examples.jp: だから言ったでしょう。
examples.en: That's what I told you, isn't it?
examples.furi: だから<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったでしょう。

related: Plain or polite form + から

meaning: and then / so / as a result

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: それで is a sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'and then / so / as a result'. It connects a previous event or reason to a consequent event or action, but with a more narrative / sequential feel than だから. Often used to introduce the next step in a story or to prompt someone to continue ('and then?'). More neutral tone than だから.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: [Previous sentence]. それで [current sentence].

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
More narrative / sequential than だから — 'and then as a result'.
In conversation, それで? alone prompts the listener to continue their story ('and then?').
Distinct from それから (which is more purely temporal 'after that').
Often used when narrating past events.

examples.jp: 電車が遅れました。それで、会議に遅刻しました。
examples.en: The train was delayed. As a result, I was late to the meeting.
examples.furi: <ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れました。それで、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>しました。

examples.jp: 昨日は疲れていました。それで、早く寝ました。
examples.en: I was tired yesterday. So I went to bed early.
examples.furi: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れていました。それで、<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ました。

examples.jp: それで、どうしましたか。
examples.en: And then, what happened?
examples.furi: それで、どうしましたか。

related: Plain or polite form + から

meaning: and then / after that / in addition

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: それから is a sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'and then / after that / in addition'. It is primarily temporal (sequential), but can also list additional items ('and another thing'). It is more purely sequential than それで (which carries a causal flavor). Common in narrating actions in order and in enumerating items.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: [Previous sentence]. それから [current sentence].

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
More temporal / sequential than それで — pure 'after that'.
Can also mean 'in addition / and also' when enumerating items.
Distinct from その後 (more neutral 'after that', formal).
Often introduces the second or subsequent step in a routine description.

examples.jp: 朝ごはんを食べました。それから、学校へ行きました。
examples.en: I ate breakfast. After that, I went to school.
examples.furi: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べました。それから、<ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きました。

examples.jp: パンを買いました。それから、牛乳も買いました。
examples.en: I bought bread. And also, I bought milk.
examples.furi: パンを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。それから、<ruby>牛乳<rt>ぎゅうにゅう</rt></ruby>も<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。

examples.jp: 宿題をして、それから、寝ます。
examples.en: I'll do my homework, and after that, sleep.
examples.furi: <ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>をして、それから、<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ます。

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: しかし is a formal / written sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'but' or 'however'. It is more formal than でも (casual but) and carries a more emphatic contrastive feeling. Common in essays, news articles, and formal speech. In casual conversation でも is preferred.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: [Previous sentence]. しかし [current sentence].

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Register: formal / written. でも is the casual equivalent.
Common in essays, editorials, news articles, and formal speech.
More emphatic than でも — often signals a significant contrast or reversal.
Related but distinct: ところが ('however / unexpectedly'), だが (slightly more literary).

examples.jp: 雨が降っていた。しかし、試合は行われた。
examples.en: It was raining. However, the match was held.
examples.furi: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>お</rt></ruby>っていた。しかし、<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>行<rt>ぎょう</rt></ruby>われた。

examples.jp: 彼は若い。しかし、経験が豊富だ。
examples.en: He is young. However, he has abundant experience.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>い。しかし、<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>豊富<rt>ほうふ</rt></ruby>だ。

examples.jp: 勉強した。しかし、試験に落ちた。
examples.en: I studied. But I failed the exam.
examples.furi: <ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>した。しかし、<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ちた。

related: Clause + が / けど / けれども

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: けれども is a more formal variant of けど ('but'), used in writing or polite spoken contexts. It can appear mid-sentence as a clausal connector (similar to が) or sentence-initially as a conjunction. Less formal than しかし but more formal than けど / けれど. The casual chain けど → けれど → けれども increases in formality.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Clause + けれども + clause (mid-sentence); or sentence-initial: [Previous]. けれども, [current].

sections.label: Register
sections.html: formal

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
The formality chain: けど (casual) < けれど < けれども < しかし (formal/written).
Can appear mid-sentence (contrastive connector) or sentence-initial (conjunction).
Interchangeable with が in most contexts, though けれども is slightly more informal than a formal が.
Common in polite spoken Japanese.

examples.jp: 雨が降っていたけれども、試合は行われた。
examples.en: Although it was raining, the match was held.
examples.furi: <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>お</rt></ruby>っていたけれども、<ruby>試合<rt>しあい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>行<rt>ぎょう</rt></ruby>われた。

examples.jp: 高いけれども、品質はいい。
examples.en: It's expensive, but the quality is good.
examples.furi: <ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いけれども、<ruby>品質<rt>ひんしつ</rt></ruby>はいい。

examples.jp: 彼は若いけれども、しっかりしている。
examples.en: He is young, but he's very solid/reliable.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>若<rt>わか</rt></ruby>いけれども、しっかりしている。

related: Clause + が / けど / けれども

meaning: like X and Y / things like (non-exhaustive casual listing)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜とか is a casual particle for non-exhaustive listing — 'like X and Y (and others)'. It is the casual counterpart of や (which lists similar items) and も〜も (which lists together). The final とか is optional and softens the listing. Common in casual speech for giving examples without being exhaustive.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Noun + とか (+ noun + とか) + main clause. Can also follow verbs in plain form: 食べるとか寝るとか.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Casual — more common in spoken Japanese than in writing.
Compare with や (slightly more formal, for noun listing): 映画や音楽が好きです vs 映画とか音楽とか好き.
Can list actions by attaching to verb plain forms: 食べるとか飲むとか.
Optional final とか softens and opens the list: X とか Y とか (implying there's more).

examples.jp: スポーツとか音楽とかが好きです。
examples.en: I like things like sports and music.
examples.furi: スポーツとか<ruby>音楽<rt>おんがく</rt></ruby>とかが<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きです。

examples.jp: 映画を見るとか、買い物するとかしましょう。
examples.en: Let's do things like watch a movie or go shopping.
examples.furi: <ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るとか、<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>するとかしましょう。

examples.jp: りんごとかバナナとかを買いました。
examples.en: I bought things like apples and bananas.
examples.furi: りんごとかバナナとかを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いました。

related: Verb-た + り + Verb-た + り + する
Plain form + し (+ plain form + し + ...)

meaning: (casual) that... / they said... / the thing called...

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜って is a highly versatile casual particle with three main uses: (1) casual quotation — equivalent to と (彼は来るって言った 'he said he'll come'); (2) topic marker — emphasizing or introducing a topic (日本語って難しい 'Japanese is hard'); (3) casual という ('called') for naming (佐藤って人 'a person called Sato'). It is strictly casual and should not be used in formal writing.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form clause / phrase + って.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: casual

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Three main uses: quotation, topic marker, 'called'.
All casual — replace with the formal equivalents (と, は, という) in polite speech.
Quotation sense: 〜って言う ('to say ~').
Naming sense: 〜って人 / 〜ってもの ('a person / thing called ~').

examples.jp: 彼は明日来るって言ってた。
examples.en: He said he'll come tomorrow.
examples.furi: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るって<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた。

examples.jp: 日本語って難しいね。
examples.en: Japanese is hard, isn't it?
examples.furi: <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>語って<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しいね。

examples.jp: 佐藤って人を知ってる？
examples.en: Do you know someone called Sato?
examples.furi: 佐藤って<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>ってる？

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: それでも is a sentence-initial conjunction meaning 'even so / nonetheless'. It concedes the previous statement and presents a contrasting main clause. More emphatic than でも when used at the start of a new sentence — it acknowledges the previous point but insists on the following. Common in arguments and opinion statements.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: [Previous sentence]. それでも [current sentence].

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Concessive — acknowledges the previous point before presenting a contrast.
More emphatic than bare でも at sentence start.
Commonly used with resolve or determination: それでも諦めない ('even so, I won't give up').
Compare to しかし (general contrast) and でも (general casual contrast).

examples.jp: 疲れている。それでも、続けなければならない。
examples.en: I'm tired. Even so, I have to continue.
examples.furi: <ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れている。それでも、<ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>けなければならない。

examples.jp: 失敗した。それでも、諦めない。
examples.en: I failed. Still, I won't give up.
examples.furi: <ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>した。それでも、<ruby>諦<rt>あきら</rt></ruby>めない。

examples.jp: 難しい。それでも、やってみる価値がある。
examples.en: It's difficult. Nonetheless, it's worth trying.
examples.furi: <ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい。それでも、やってみる<ruby>価値<rt>かち</rt></ruby>がある。

point: Verb-stem / い-adj stem / な-adj root + そう(だ/です)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: そうだ attached to a verb stem, い-adjective stem, or na-adjective root expresses a judgment based on appearance — 'it looks like', 'it seems'. The speaker is making an inference from visual or situational evidence, not reporting something they heard. This is structurally distinct from the hearsay そうだ which attaches to plain form.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Verb ます-stem + そう; い-adj drop い + そう (高い → 高そう); な-adj root + そう (元気 → 元気そう). Exceptions: いい → よさそう, ない → なさそう.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
For verbs, use the ます-stem: 食べる → 食べそう, 降る → 降りそう.
Negative of verb appearance: 〜そうにない / 〜そうもない (doesn't look like).
Negative of い-adjective appearance: 〜くなさそう (高くない → 高くなさそう).
Functions as a な-adjective grammatically: おいしそうな料理, 元気そうに見える.

examples.jp: 雨が降りそうです。
examples.en: It looks like it's going to rain.

related: Plain form / noun + みたい(だ/です)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: When そうだ attaches to a plain-form predicate (not a verb stem), it expresses hearsay — 'I heard that ___'. The speaker is reporting information received from another source rather than making their own judgment. The source can be named with 〜によると ('according to ___'). Structurally distinct from appearance-based そうだ, which attaches to the verb stem.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: Plain-form verb / i-adj / na-adj / noun + だ (for nouns and na-adj) + そうだ. Examples: 食べるそうだ, 食べたそうだ, 高いそうだ, 学生だそうだ, 元気だそうだ.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Note: for nouns and na-adjectives, the だ is retained before そうだ (学生だそうだ, not 学生そうだ — the latter would be an appearance-based construction).
No distinct past form for the hearsay そうだ itself — the tense is inside the reported clause (食べたそうだ = 'I heard they ate').
Cannot be negated as a whole unit — negate the reported content instead (来ないそうだ = 'I heard they're not coming').
The source of the hearsay is commonly introduced with 〜によると or 〜の話では.

examples.jp: 天気予報によると、明日は雨だそうです。

related: Verb-stem / い-adj stem / な-adj root + そう(だ/です)

sections.label: Meaning
sections.html: 〜ようかと思う expresses that the speaker is considering doing X, but with some hesitation or uncertainty — 'thinking of doing X / half-considering'. Less committed than 〜ようと思う (intend to do). Often used for tentative plans. Neutral / formal register.

sections.label: Formation
sections.html: V volitional + かと思う.

sections.label: Register
sections.html: neutral

sections.label: Usage
sections.html:
Tentative consideration — less committed than 〜ようと思う.
Similar to 〜ようと思っている but with the か adding doubt.
Common in tentative planning: 留学しようかと思っている.
Neutral register.
